Processes

Every program that we write is represented as a process in the OS when we run it.

"A process is a program in execution"

A single program's execution can be characterized by a trace of the instructions that are executed.

The OS scheduler is responsible for deciding which process gets to use the CPU at any given time and for how long.

What happens to a process when it is not running? It sits in a queue waiting to get its opportunity to run again.

One can think of a process as going through a series of states during its lifetime.

PCB

What information does an OS need to control processes and manage resources for them?

What is a process's state?

Process Control Block (PCB) is a data structure that contains all the information about a process that the OS needs to manage it.

Whenever a process gives up the CPU we have to store the contents of the CPU registers so that when the process gets to run again the registers can be reloaded.

Recall that a process can be running or ready.

If a process requests some I/O operation then it should be blocked so that the other processes can use the CPU to make progress.

  • Running: a process has the processor and is executing instructions.
  • Ready: a process does not have the processor but it could run if the OS scheduler dispatched it.
  • Blocked: process does not have the processor and could not run even if the processor was available.

If you think of a simple program when waiting for the user to enter in information the process should definitely block itself so that other processes can use the CPU.

Short Term Scheduling

A short term scheduler is responsible for deciding which process in the ready state should be dispatched to the CPU next.

Long Term Scheduling

A long term scheduler is responsible for deciding when a new process should be admitted into the ready state.

  • New: a new process is created in the system.
  • Exit: a process has completed its work.

If there are many new processes the long term scheduler may decided to delay admitting some of them into the ready state until there is more memory available.

When a process exits, the OS will free the RAM associated with it making it more likely that the long term scheduler will admit new processes into the ready state.

Medium Term Scheduling

Since memory is finite, the OS also has a medium term scheduler that is responsible for swapping out (to the disk) processes that are blocked on I/O so that memory can be used for other non-blocked processes.

This introduces a couple of suspended states.

If there are no processes in the ready state but there are some processes in the ready suspended state, the medium term scheduler can swap one of those processes back into memory and move it to the ready state so that it can be dispatched by the short term scheduler.

Summary of Schedulers

Architectures

Multi-programming: multiple processes are in memory at the same time and the OS scheduler interleaves their execution on the a single CPU.

This was the most common architecture for computers when there was a single CPU per computer.

Now, we have multiple CPUs per computer (even in our phones and tablets). When we take advantage of mulitple processors we call it multiprocessing.

Symetrical Multiprocessing (SMP): multiple CPUs that share memory. The OS can run on any of the CPUs and can dispatch processes to any of the CPUs.

Asymmetrical Multiprocessing (AMP): multiple CPUs that are different and do not share memory.

Since the processes don't share memory when they need to communicate with each other they have to use some form of inter-process communication (IPC) like message passing.
